chunks: Aban narrated from Abu al-Jarud, who said:

Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: A man should not buy what he has given in charity. And if he gives a dwelling in charity to a relative, if he wishes, he may live with them. And if he gives a servant in charity to a relative, the servant serves him if he wishes.

As for what Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal narrated from Amr ibn Uthman from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira from Talhah ibn Zayd from Abu Abdillah from his father (peace be upon him) that a man gave his house in charity while he was living in it, so he said, 'Leave it,' when he exited from it. This does not contradict the first report, because the meaning of his command to leave the house was only to validate the endowment (waqf), because we have explained that part of its validity is handing over the endowment to the one upon whom it is endowed, and the purpose was not that it was forbidden for him to be prohibited, and this does not contradict that.

What Ali ibn al-Hasan narrated from Ya'qub ibn Yazid al-Katib from Ibn Abi Umayr from Abu al-Maghra from Abu Basir from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him about the charity of what has not been received and not divided. He said: It is permissible, because the meaning in this report is that the charity of what has not been received is permissible, and we did not say that it is not permissible, but we said that fulfilling it is not obligatory, and its owner is free to choose in that matter.
ai.seo_question: Can a donor buy back their charity or continue living in a house they gave in charity?
ai.summary: This excerpt from *Al-Istibsar* clarifies the distinction between *sadaqah* (gift/charity) and *waqf* (endowment) in Shia jurisprudence, emphasizing that a donor retains the right to repurchase their charity or continue using it if given to a relative. The text resolves apparent contradictions in prophetic traditions by interpreting commands to 'leave' a house as a mechanism for transferring possession to validate the endowment, rather than imposing a permanent prohibition on the donor's residence. Furthermore, it establishes that charity given before full possession is valid but not strictly binding, granting the donor discretion in fulfillment.
